Arithmetic with known precision

Source: R/arith.R
precision-arithmetic.Rd

Results are calculated using the full values. The precision of the result is the coarsest known precision of the inputs, so 3.2 + 4.12 is 7.3. Ordinary numbers are exact, and don't affect the precision of the result.

Details

Arithmetic

+, -, *, /, ^, %% and %/% use the coarsest known precision of each pair of elements. Inputs must be the same size, or size 1.

Summaries

sum(), prod(), mean(), min(), max(), range(), median() and quantile() use the coarsest known precision of all elements (excluding missing values if na.rm = TRUE).

Cumulative

cumsum(), cumprod(), cummin() and cummax() use the coarsest known precision of the elements so far.

Rounding

round() and signif() round the value, and the precision becomes no finer than the digits rounded to. floor(), ceiling() and trunc() similarly reduce known precision to no finer than 0, while exact numbers remain exact. sign() is exact.

Other functions

exp(), log(), sqrt(), abs() and so on keep the precision of their input.

The result's precision is missing only if it is missing for all inputs. Logical operators (&, |, !, any(), all()) are not supported, and is.na(), is.nan(), is.finite() and is.infinite() give logical vectors based only on the value.

Base R finds methods for functions like sum() with their first argument, so use sum(x, 1) instead of sum(1, x).

Examples

precision(3.2, 1) + precision(4.12, 2)
#> <precision[1]>
#> [1] 7.3
precision(3.2, 1) * 2
#> <precision[1]>
#> [1] 6.4
sum(precision(c(1.234, 5.6), c(3, 1)))
#> <precision[1]>
#> [1] 6.8
cumsum(precision(c(1.234, 5.6, 7.89), c(3, 1, 2)))
#> <precision[3]>
#> [1] 1.234   6.8  14.7
round(precision(3.14159, 5), 2)
#> <precision[1]>
#> [1] 3.14
